theory.intro: **Network diagrams** model real-world systems such as roads, delivery routes, and pipelines. Solving network problems involves calculating total travel times or distances along routes, comparing paths, and finding paths that meet practical constraints.
facts: The **total weight of a path** is the sum of the weights of its edges: $\text{Weight}(A\text{–}B\text{–}C) = w(AB) + w(BC)$.
A **path** is a walk that visits no vertex and no edge more than once.
In a **directed network**, any valid route must travel only in the direction of the edge arrows.
The **out-capacity or departures** from a vertex is the sum of weights on all edges leaving that vertex.
The shortest route between two vertices is the path with the smallest sum of edge weights.
A **closed path or tour** is a route that starts and finishes at the same vertex, visiting required vertices in between.
steps: Trace the sequence of vertices along valid edges
Sum the weights of the traversed edges
Compare candidate routes or interpret the total in context

foundation.question_text:
A network diagram represents water flow through pipes between four storage tanks.
Explain what the vertices, edges, and edge weights represent in this context.
foundation.solution_text:
Vertices represent the storage tanks or pipe junctions.
Edges represent the connecting water pipes.
Edge weights represent the flow capacity (e.g. litres per minute) or pipe length.

foundation.question_text:
A delivery van can take the North Highway ($18\text{ km} + 24\text{ km}$) or the South Bypass ($15\text{ km} + 22\text{ km}$) from Warehouse to Retail Store.
Calculate the distance saved by taking the shorter route.
foundation.solution_text:
$\text{North Highway} = 18 + 24 = 42\text{ km}$
$\text{South Bypass} = 15 + 22 = 37\text{ km}$
$\text{Distance saved} = 42 - 37$
$= 5\text{ km}$

development.question_text:
A municipal pump station supplies three water districts through separate mains with rated capacities of $350\text{ L/min}$, $480\text{ L/min}$, and $520\text{ L/min}$.
What is the maximum volume of water, in litres, that can be pumped out of the station in $2\text{ hours}$?
development.solution_text:
$\text{Total rate} = 350 + 480 + 520 = 1350\text{ L/min}$
$\text{Time in minutes} = 2 \times 60 = 120\text{ min}$
$\text{Volume} = 1350 \times 120$
$= 162\,000\text{ L}$

mastery.question_text:
A sales manager starts at Base $A$, visits four regional branches $B, C, D, E$, and returns to $A$.
Two candidate closed tours have the following edge distances in km:
Tour 1 ($A\text{–}B\text{–}C\text{–}D\text{–}E\text{–}A$): $24 + 32 + 28 + 45 + 51 = 180\text{ km}$
Tour 2 ($A\text{–}C\text{–}E\text{–}D\text{–}B\text{–}A$): $38 + 29 + 45 + 36 + 24 = 172\text{ km}$
If travel allowance is paid at $\$0.85\text{ per km}$, calculate the cost saving of Tour 2 over Tour 1.

A freight ship routes cargo between ports $A$ and $E$.
Route 1 ($A\to B\to E$) requires $28\text{ h}$ sailing plus $12\text{ h}$ port delay at $B$.
Route 2 ($A\to C\to D\to E$) requires $16\text{ h} + 14\text{ h} + 11\text{ h} = 41\text{ h}$ sailing plus $4\text{ h}$ delay at $C$ and $4\text{ h}$ delay at $D$.
Determine which route is faster and state whether it arrives within a $50\text{-hour}$ delivery window.
mastery.solution_text:
$\text{Route 1 total} = 28 + 12 = 40\text{ hours}$
$\text{Route 2 total} = 41 + 4 + 4 = 49\text{ hours}$
Route 1 is faster ($40\text{ hours}$); both routes arrive within the $50\text{-hour}$ window.

mastery.question_text:
A bus terminal has three arriving feeder routes delivering passengers at rates of $180$, $240$, and $310\text{ passengers/hour}$.
Two departing express routes can carry a maximum of $350$ and $420\text{ passengers/hour}$.
Calculate the total incoming versus outgoing capacity, and determine whether passenger congestion will build up over a $3\text{-hour}$ peak period.
mastery.solution_text:
$\text{Incoming capacity} = 180 + 240 + 310 = 730\text{ passengers/hour}$
$\text{Outgoing capacity} = 350 + 420 = 770\text{ passengers/hour}$
Since $770 > 730$, outgoing capacity exceeds arrivals by $40\text{ passengers/hour}$.
No congestion will build up because departure capacity ($770/\text{h}$) exceeds arrival rate ($730/\text{h}$).
